title: A Label Is Not a Wire

scenes.tts: How does a brain wire itself, partner by partner? Start with one small circuit.
scenes.visual: Title fades. A question card: How does a brain wire itself? A leg in profile, a reflex hammer poised below the knee.
scenes.narration: How does a brain wire itself, partner by partner? Start with one small circuit.

scenes.tts: Tap the tendon below the knee, and the leg kicks.
scenes.visual: The hammer taps the tendon below the kneecap; the lower leg swings forward.
scenes.narration: Tap the tendon below the knee, and the leg kicks.

scenes.tts: A sensory neuron in the thigh muscle excites the motor neurons of that same muscle.
scenes.visual: Cut-away of the thigh and spinal cord. A sensory axon (blue) runs from a spindle in the front thigh muscle into the cord and contacts motor neurons of the same muscle. A green plus sign marks the synapse. Label: quadriceps.
scenes.narration: A sensory neuron in the thigh muscle excites the motor neurons of that same muscle.

scenes.tts: Through an inhibitory interneuron, it also quiets the motor neurons of the opposing muscle.
scenes.visual: The same sensory axon contacts a small interneuron (grey), which contacts motor neurons of the back thigh muscle. A red minus sign marks that synapse. Label: hamstring.
scenes.narration: Through an inhibitory interneuron, it also quiets the motor neurons of the opposing muscle.

scenes.tts: The right partners, with the right signs. Development built every one of those connections.
scenes.visual: The plus and minus signs pulse. Caption on screen: right partner, right sign.
scenes.narration: The right partners, with the right signs. Development built every one of those connections.

scenes.tts: Now scale up. A human brain has about eighty-six billion neurons.
scenes.caption: Now scale up. A human brain has about 86 billion neurons.
scenes.visual: The reflex circuit shrinks to a dot and the view pulls back to a whole brain. Counter 1: 86 billion neurons.
scenes.narration: Now scale up. A human brain has about 86 billion neurons.

scenes.tts: They are joined by something like a hundred trillion synapses.
scenes.caption: They are joined by something like 100 trillion synapses.
scenes.visual: Counter 2: about 100 trillion synapses (10^14 on screen only).
scenes.narration: They are joined by something like 100 trillion synapses.

scenes.tts: The genome that builds them has about twenty thousand protein-coding genes.
scenes.caption: The genome that builds them has about 20,000 protein-coding genes.
scenes.visual: Counter 3: about 20,000 protein-coding genes. A DNA double helix beside it.
scenes.narration: The genome that builds them has about 20,000 protein-coding genes.

scenes.tts: Could the genome simply list the connections?
scenes.visual: A long scroll labelled wiring list unrolls beside a short strip labelled whole genome.
scenes.narration: Could the genome simply list the connections?

scenes.tts: Even using every letter of the genome, the list would be about a million times too long.
scenes.visual: The wiring-list bar stretches far off screen; the genome is a sliver. On-screen only: list ~ 4 x 10^15 bits; genome ~ 6 x 10^9 bits; ~10^6 too big.
scenes.narration: Even using every letter of the genome, the list would be about a million times too long.

scenes.tts: So is the trouble giving every neuron its own name?
scenes.visual: A single neuron with a blank name tag. Question card: Is naming the problem?
scenes.narration: So is the trouble giving every neuron its own name?

scenes.tts: No. Names are cheap. Each extra on-off gene doubles the number of combinations.
scenes.visual: A row of on-off switches. Each switch added doubles a counter: 2, 4, 8, 16 ... The counter races past 86 billion at 37 switches.
scenes.narration: No. Names are cheap. Each extra on-off gene doubles the number of combinations.

scenes.tts: A few dozen genes could give every neuron its own name.
scenes.visual: Every neuron in a crowd receives a distinct coloured name tag.
scenes.narration: A few dozen genes could give every neuron its own name.

scenes.tts: But a name says which cell you are. It does not say whom to connect to.
scenes.visual: One tagged neuron; a question mark hovers over a cloud of billions of possible partners.
scenes.narration: But a name says which cell you are. It does not say whom to connect to.

scenes.tts: A label is not a wire.
scenes.visual: Text card: A label is not a wire.
scenes.narration: A label is not a wire.

scenes.tts: So the genome stores rules. The first is a graded label.
scenes.visual: Card: Rule 1, graded labels. The retina appears as a disc, shaded light to dark.
scenes.narration: So the genome stores rules. The first is a graded label.

scenes.tts: Retinal ganglion cells carry a receptor whose amount depends on where they sit in the eye.
scenes.visual: Retina disc coloured by receptor level, high at one edge and low at the other. Label: EphA receptor.
scenes.narration: Retinal ganglion cells carry a receptor whose amount depends on where they sit in the eye.

scenes.tts: Their target in the brain carries the matching cue, in an opposing gradient.
scenes.visual: The midbrain target appears, shaded the opposite way. Label: ephrin-A cue.
scenes.narration: Their target in the brain carries the matching cue, in an opposing gradient.

scenes.tts: The second is a local rule. Each growing tip, the growth cone, reads only what is right next to it.
scenes.visual: Card: Rule 2, local rules. Zoom on one axon tip with fine fingers sampling the cue just around it.
scenes.narration: The second is a local rule. Each growing tip, the growth cone, reads only what is right next to it.

scenes.tts: Axons with more receptor are kept away from places with more cue.
scenes.visual: Many growth cones advance; those rich in receptor turn back from the high-cue region and settle where cue is low.
scenes.narration: Axons with more receptor are kept away from places with more cue.

scenes.tts: In our toy model, each axon settles where receptor times cue reaches a set threshold. That rule and the opposing gradients give the right overall order. Real maps also use competition, and more cues.
scenes.visual: Corner label: toy model. Inset on the model diagram: receptor × cue = threshold, with one axon stopping where its product line crosses the threshold. Axon endings line up across the target with colours in roughly the same order as in the retina; neighbouring growth cones jostle one another.
scenes.narration: In our toy model, each axon settles where receptor times cue reaches a set threshold. That rule and the opposing gradients give the right overall order. Real maps also use competition, and more cues.

scenes.tts: Now take two hundred evenly spaced axons and a tenfold gradient. Suppose each reading has an independent random error of about ten percent. In this toy model, overall order stays high, but neighbouring pairs land in the right order only about fifty-three percent of the time.
scenes.visual: Corner label: simple model, not measured anatomy. Display: N = 200; F = 10; σ = 0.1; illustrative model. 200 small landing-point markers scattered around their ideal positions across the target, with some adjacent colours swapped. No arbor shapes are drawn; any spread shown is labelled as possible positions across repeated trials, not arbor width.
scenes.narration: Now take 200 evenly spaced axons and a tenfold gradient. Suppose each reading has an independent random error of about 10 percent. In this toy model, overall order stays high, but neighbouring pairs land in the right order only about 53 percent of the time.
scenes.caption: Now take 200 evenly spaced axons and a tenfold gradient. Suppose each reading has an independent random error of about 10 percent. In this toy model, overall order stays high, but neighbouring pairs land in the right order only about 53 percent of the time.

scenes.tts: A third rule sharpens that: overproduce, then select.
scenes.visual: Card: Rule 3, overproduce, then select.
scenes.narration: A third rule sharpens that: overproduce, then select.

scenes.tts: Each axon branches more widely than it needs.
scenes.visual: Each axon ending sprouts many branches spread over a wide area of the target.
scenes.narration: Each axon branches more widely than it needs.

scenes.tts: Neighbouring cells in the retina tend to fire together.
scenes.visual: In the retina, neighbouring cells flash at the same moment, a wave of flashes sweeping across.
scenes.narration: Neighbouring cells in the retina tend to fire together.

scenes.tts: A branch among its retinal neighbours fires in step with them, and together they drive the same target cells. Such branches tend to stay. Branches among strangers tend to retract.
scenes.visual: One target neuron receives several converging branches. Branches that flash in step with the others there drive it and usually thicken; an out-of-step branch more often fades and retracts. Over time the arbors tighten into small, ordered patches.
scenes.narration: A branch among its retinal neighbours fires in step with them, and together they drive the same target cells. Such branches tend to stay. Branches among strangers tend to retract.

scenes.tts: The tissue measures this after the connections form, so the genome never has to store it.
scenes.visual: The tightened map holds; a small DNA icon is shown with a cross through a long list.
scenes.narration: The tissue measures this after the connections form, so the genome never has to store it.

scenes.tts: Here is a test. A goldfish can regrow a cut optic nerve.
scenes.visual: A goldfish; its optic nerve shown cut, then axons regrowing toward the brain.
scenes.narration: Here is a test. A goldfish can regrow a cut optic nerve.

scenes.tts: Block every spike from its eye with tetrodotoxin while the axons grow back.
scenes.visual: A stamp on the eye: tetrodotoxin, no spikes. Spike traces from the eye go flat.
scenes.narration: Block every spike from its eye with tetrodotoxin while the axons grow back.

scenes.tts: Which part of the map survives: the rough order, or the fine precision?
scenes.visual: Question card with two boxes: rough order? fine precision?
scenes.narration: Which part of the map survives: the rough order, or the fine precision?

scenes.tts: The axons still reached their target, in roughly the right order.
scenes.visual: Split screen. Left, untreated fish: tight endings in order. Right, tetrodotoxin: endings in the same rough order.
scenes.narration: The axons still reached their target, in roughly the right order.

scenes.tts: But their branches stayed spread over a wide area, instead of clustering tightly.
scenes.visual: Right panel: each ending stays wide and blurred, overlapping its neighbours. The rough order box ticks; the fine precision box crosses.
scenes.narration: But their branches stayed spread over a wide area, instead of clustering tightly.

scenes.tts: Molecular cues probably placed them. Activity sharpened them.
scenes.visual: Two labels appear over the split screen: cues, rough order; activity, sharp endings.
scenes.narration: Molecular cues probably placed them. Activity sharpened them.

scenes.tts: Now block spikes in zebrafish embryos, as their first map forms. The map formed in order, and single arbors stayed small and tight.
scenes.visual: Inset: a zebrafish embryo with the no-spikes stamp; its retinal map forms in order, with small, tight endings like an untreated embryo.
scenes.narration: Now block spikes in zebrafish embryos, as their first map forms. The map formed in order, and single arbors stayed small and tight.

scenes.tts: So the line can fall in different places. But these fish also differ in age, and in regrowing a map versus building one.
scenes.visual: Two labelled cards side by side. Regrowing adult goldfish: order kept, endings wide. Developing zebrafish embryo: order kept, endings small.
scenes.narration: So the line can fall in different places. But these fish also differ in age, and in regrowing a map versus building one.

scenes.tts: The takeaway: the genome stores rules, and the tissue measures the rest.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: The genome stores rules, and the tissue measures the rest.
scenes.narration: The takeaway: the genome stores rules, and the tissue measures the rest.

scenes.tts: The course follows those rules in three acts: where cells go, how axons find their targets, and who survives.
scenes.visual: Three act cards slide in: 1 where cells go; 2 how axons find their targets; 3 who survives.
scenes.narration: The course follows those rules in three acts: where cells go, how axons find their targets, and who survives.
